function.mechanism: Conjugated double-bond chromophore absorbs visible light to impart yellow-orange color; can be cleaved to vitamin A.

adi.basis: EFSA 2012 additive re-evaluation did not establish an ADI; concluded no safety concern for current food-additive uses under assessed exposure conditions.

efsa.key_finding: No safety concern was identified for current uses/levels of E160a from food additives; concern context is high supplemental exposure in heavy smokers.

adi.basis: JECFA (2019) withdrew prior group ADIs (historically 0-5 mg/kg bw/day) and could not establish a group ADI applicable to the general population including heavy smokers.

concerns.summary: Supplemental beta-carotene is associated with increased lung cancer risk in smokers in randomized-trial evidence syntheses; meta-analysis of RCTs reported elevated lung cancer risk (RR about 1.19).
Mechanistic literature indicates smoke co-exposure plus high supplemental doses may increase oxidative beta-carotene metabolite formation and pro-proliferative signaling.

no_concern_confirmed: EFSA reported no safety concern for E160a at current food-additive uses and levels assessed.
FDA allows use under GMP as a color additive and affirms GRAS direct-food use under listed conditions.
Dietary (food-source) antioxidant patterns are not consistently associated with harm and may be protective in observational datasets.

adi_exceedance.notes: EFSA statement estimated typical total intake from diet plus additives generally below ~15 mg/day; risk signal is tied to supplemental intakes (e.g., 20-30 mg/day in smoker trials) rather than ordinary additive exposure.

risk_assessment.rationale: Regulatory approvals remain in place for food-additive use, but credible smoker-specific carcinogenic risk signals at supplemental doses and JECFA ADI withdrawal prevent a low-concern classification.
key_factors: EFSA 2012 additive re-evaluation found no concern at current additive exposure levels
FDA CFR status is permitted/GRAS under GMP conditions
JECFA withdrew prior group ADI in 2019
RCT/meta-analytic evidence shows increased lung cancer risk with supplemental beta-carotene in smokers
No IARC classification for beta-carotene found in checked classification resources
